confirmed.evidence: `var request = URLRequest(url: URL(string: urlString)!)` at :127 is fully constructed (including an `await applyHeaders` token round-trip) and never sent. `let directURL = "\(baseURL)/rest/v1/products?id=eq.\(id)&select=\(Self.productSelect)"` then force-unwraps URL(string:) at :134 — a deep link or push carrying a malformed piece id becomes a crash rather than a 'not found'. These are the only URL force-unwraps outside config literals (11 total).
confirmed.fix: Delete the dead request; build the second with URLComponents/URLQueryItem as fetchProducts(ids:) already does on the next function, and drop the !.
confirmed.codeNote: Both halves are code-true at the exact lines: ProductAPIClient.swift:126 builds `URLRequest(url: URL(string: urlString)!)` for rpc/get_recommendations?p_limit=1, sets httpMethod, runs `await applyHeaders`, and never sends it; :133-134 interpolate the raw id into directURL and force-unwrap URL(string:). Two calibrations. testerVisible should be false: the dead request is invisible, and the crash needs a deliberately malformed piece id — a well-formed uuid always parses, and since iOS 17 Foundation parses the interpolated select clause's commas, parens and `!` without complaint. And the finding names the wrong cost: the real user-facing one is that the dead request still awaits auth.session.accessToken on every piece-detail open, an avoidable token round-trip on the app's most-opened screen. The '11 total' force-unwrap count reads 12 by grep under Patina/ — incidental.
confirmed.judgeNote: Adjusted testerVisible from true to false. No first-round tester reaches the crash under normal use: the interpolated id arrives from a universal link that is already percent-encoded, so URL(string:) returning nil needs a hand-mangled link. That is latent hardening, not a visible defect, and it should not compete with tester-facing work. What DOES earn week one is the dead code beside it — a fully built URLRequest including an `await applyHeaders` token round-trip, constructed and discarded on every single-product fetch, i.e. an avoidable auth hop on the exact path that opens the product detail. Fix both in one S change; the perf argument, not the crash argument, is why it is T1 and not T2.

confirmed.title: NetworkError is effectively dead and its descriptions are developer copy
confirmed.evidence: Two call sites app-wide (grep 'NetworkError.'), yet errorDescription reads 'Failed to decode response: \(error.localizedDescription)' and 'Server error (\(statusCode)): ...'. If anything starts surfacing it, those are raw strings on a tester's screen.
confirmed.fix: Delete it, or give it Patina copy before it acquires readers.
confirmed.codeNote: Developer copy confirmed verbatim (NetworkError.swift:22-43: 'Invalid URL', 'Failed to decode response: \(…)', 'Server error (\(statusCode)): …', 'You are not authorized to perform this action'). Correction to the evidence: there is exactly ONE call site app-wide, not two — AuthService.swift:366 `throw NetworkError.unauthorized` on the Sign-in-with-Apple missing-id-token path. That path is user-reachable, so 'effectively dead' slightly understates it: a caller that surfaces localizedDescription would print developer copy during Apple sign-in.
confirmed.judgeNote: Correctly marked not tester-visible — two call sites, effectively dead. The value here is preventive: 'Failed to decode response: …' and 'Server error (500): …' are raw developer strings sitting one wiring change away from a tester's screen, in a codebase that has already been burned by exactly that (see the Stripe key leak the OrderFailureCopy header documents). Delete the type rather than rewriting copy for a dead path. T2.

confirmed.title: The persistent scan queue gives up after three tries, with no backoff and no way for the tester to know or retry
confirmed.evidence: `canRetry: retryCount < 3` and a fixed `try? await Task.sleep(nanoseconds: 500_000_000)` between items — no exponential backoff. Three consecutive failures (a bad tunnel, an expired token per C7-15) park the row permanently. pendingUploads counts it but nothing offers a retry and nothing tells the person the scan never left the phone.
confirmed.fix: Exponential backoff, a higher cap, and a surfaced 'this scan hasn't been sent' state with a retry.
confirmed.codeNote: Mechanism refuted, conclusion confirmed and worse than stated — so adjusted rather than refuted. The queue the finding cites is DEAD: SyncQueueItem.create is called only from RoomScanSyncService.queueUploadPersistent (:326-355), and `grep -rn queueUploadPersistent` over the app returns only its own declaration — zero call sites. queueUpload (:280) is likewise called only from inside that dead function. So no scan ever enters the SyncQueueItem queue and the `retryCount < 3` cap at SyncQueueItem.swift:103-105 is never reached. The live path is RoomScanPackage + resumePendingUploads, which has no retry cap and no backoff at all and re-fans on every launch and network transition (C7-14). The corrected, sharper defect: countPendingItems (:419-432) computes pendingUploads as the sum of those two structurally-empty queues, so YourSpacesView.swift:240-241's 'Will retry when online' pill can never render for a real scan — a tester whose scan never left the phone gets no signal whatsoever, which is exactly the outcome the finding predicts, by a different route.
confirmed.judgeNote: Raised from minor after checking what the UI actually surfaces. YourSpacesView.swift:238-244 has exactly two pill states: offline-with-pending, and isSyncing. A row parked permanently at retryCount >= 3 while ONLINE renders nothing at all — the scan silently never leaves the phone, and there is no retry affordance anywhere. From the homeowner's side that is indistinguishable from data loss on the one artefact they worked hardest for. Compounding it: the pill lives on Your Spaces, which per A1-02 is orb-only on the flags-off TestFlight root, so a build-1 tester may never see upload state in any form. Three failures with a fixed 500ms gap and no backoff is also a near-guarantee on a flaky connection. M effort; the backoff half is trivial and the surfaced 'this scan hasn't been sent' + retry is the part that matters.

confirmed.title: A detached Task per telemetry event for the PostHog mirror
confirmed.evidence: `Task.detached { await PostHogService.shared.capture(...) }` inside enqueue, which is called from viewport enter/exit and every dwell event — one detached task per event, each hopping to the main actor because PostHogService is @MainActor, during scrolling.
confirmed.fix: Batch the PostHog mirror alongside the existing 30 s flush instead of one task per event.
confirmed.codeNote: CONFIRMED exactly. DailyRoomBatchQueue.swift:55-60 is `Task.detached { await PostHogService.shared.capture(...) }` inside enqueue(_:), one detached task per event, and PostHogService is declared `@MainActor` at PostHogService.swift:14-15 so each task immediately hops to the main actor. enqueue is the viewport/dwell path, so this fires during scrolling. Batching the mirror onto the existing 30 s flush is the right fix.
confirmed.judgeNote: Scroll smoothness is a world-class signal and a main-actor hop per viewport event during scrolling is the right thing to dislike, but there is no evidence it costs a perceptible frame at current catalogue size. Same file and same queue as C7-13 — fold it into that work whenever the telemetry lane is opened, not before.

confirmed.title: Two remaining .first! force unwraps on FileManager.urls(for:in:)
confirmed.evidence: `FileManager.default.urls(for: .applicationSupportDirectory, in: .userDomainMask).first!` and the documentDirectory twin. Practically safe on iOS; still the only non-URL force unwraps left in the app.
confirmed.fix: Guard and degrade to a no-op store.
confirmed.codeNote: CONFIRMED. `grep -rn '\.first!'` across apps/mobile/Patina returns exactly two hits: DailyRoomBatchQueue.swift:22 (.applicationSupportDirectory) and ConversationStorageService.swift:237 (.documentDirectory). Supporting the 'only ones left' claim: `grep -rn 'try!'` outside PatinaTests returns nothing.
confirmed.judgeNote: Practically unreachable on iOS — applicationSupportDirectory and documentDirectory always resolve — so this is craft, not risk. Keeping it rather than cutting it: a two-line guard is cheaper than the standard it breaks, and these are the last two non-URL force unwraps in the app, so closing them buys a clean rule to enforce.

confirmed.title: DeploymentTarget is read from the whole UserDefaults search list, not just the argument domain
confirmed.evidence: `if let override = UserDefaults.standard.string(forKey: "DeploymentTarget")`. The intended `-DeploymentTarget local` lands in the volatile NSArgumentDomain, so normal use is safe — but any persisted or restored value in the app's own domain would silently point a TestFlight build at http://127.0.0.1:54321, where every request fails and every screen renders empty. Nothing in the app writes the key (grep-verified), so this is a latent shape rather than a live bug.
confirmed.fix: Read the argument domain explicitly and compile the .local branch out of Release.
confirmed.codeNote: Verified: APIConfiguration.swift:26 reads `UserDefaults.standard.string(forKey: "DeploymentTarget")` inside DeploymentTarget.current (:25-33), and a repo-wide grep for 'DeploymentTarget' across Patina/PatinaWidget/PatinaWidgetShared finds only that file — nothing writes the key, so it is latent exactly as described. The .local branch (http://127.0.0.1:54321, :51-52) is compiled into Release. The finding's own 'latent shape rather than a live bug' framing and polish grade are honest.
confirmed.judgeNote: polish→minor, on blast radius rather than probability. The finder is right that nothing writes the key, so this will almost certainly never fire — but if it ever does, a TestFlight build points at http://127.0.0.1:54321, every screen renders empty, and neither the tester nor Kody has any way to diagnose it. One-line fix (read NSArgumentDomain explicitly) plus compiling the .local branch out of Release is straightforward release hygiene. T1, not T0: no live trigger exists.

confirmed.title: The scan flow identifies its session by identifierForVendor or the literal string 'anonymous', not the signed-in user
confirmed.evidence: `private func currentUserId() -> String { UIDevice.current.identifierForVendor?.uuidString ?? "anonymous" }`, with the comment 'Supabase auth integration will provide a real user id where available.' That value becomes RoomScanSession.userId and ScanAnalytics.Context.userId, so every scan a signed-in tester makes is attributed in analytics to a device id — or to 'anonymous'. The upload path resolves the real user separately, so server rows are correct; the telemetry is not.
confirmed.fix: Read AuthService.shared.currentUserId here.
confirmed.codeNote: Exact, including the comment. QuietConversationFlowHost.swift:162-166 is `private func currentUserId() -> String { UIDevice.current.identifierForVendor?.uuidString ?? "anonymous" }` with the comment 'Supabase auth integration will provide a real user id where available.' It is passed into ScanViewModel.init (:112-128), which writes it to both `RoomScanSession(userId:)` and `ScanAnalytics.Context(userId:)`. The finding's own caveat is also right — the upload path resolves the real user separately (getCurrentUserId in the sync service), so server rows stay correct and only telemetry is wrong. One-line fix, no tester impact.
confirmed.judgeNote: Confirmed at QuietConversationFlowHost.swift:161-166 — currentUserId() returns identifierForVendor or the literal 'anonymous', and that value becomes RoomScanSession.userId and ScanAnalytics.Context.userId. testerVisible false is correct: server rows resolve the real user separately, so nothing breaks for the homeowner. Tiering it T1 anyway on program grounds — the entire point of round 1 is learning what testers do with the scan feature, and scan telemetry that will not join to a user account undercuts that. Mitigated by the fact that in a 5-20 person cohort a device id is effectively a person, which is why this is T1 and not T0. One line: read AuthService.shared.currentUserId.

confirmed.title: Today's scroll ends in 240 pt of dead canvas (root reservation + a second local 120)
confirmed.evidence: ContentView applies .companionHearthReservation to the whole NavigationStack, adding a safeAreaInset(edge:.bottom) of CompanionHearthMetrics.reservation(...) = 120 at normal text size (Design/Components/CompanionSafeArea.swift:178-186, :148-151). DailyRoomView — the flag-off root's home, where every first-round tester lands — ALSO appends `Spacer().frame(height: 120)` at the end of its column. The two stack to 240 pt above the home indicator for a dock documented at 140 (CompanionSafeArea.swift:33-40: "mark 64 + gap 4 + caption row 44 + lift 28 = 140"). ~100 pt of nothing, 27% of an 874 pt screen.
confirmed.fix: Delete the local Spacer().frame(height: 120) from DailyRoomView; the root reservation already owns this edge.
confirmed.codeNote: The double reservation is exactly as described and it IS on the round-one path: ContentView.swift:185 applies `.companionHearthReservation(isActive:)` to the legacy (flag-off) NavigationStack; `reservesRootHearth(for:houseFirst:)` defaults houseFirst to false and returns true for Today (CompanionSafeArea.swift:84-92); `reservation(accessibilityText:false)` = reservedHeight = 64+36+20 = 120 (:16-22, :148-151); and DailyRoomView.swift:371 appends a second `Spacer().frame(height: 120)`. What is overstated is the visible cost — the Companion dock draws INSIDE that region (shot R/18 shows the mark and 'NEXT STEPS' sitting in it), so the surplus at max scroll is roughly 100 pt of trailing canvas, not '240 pt of dead canvas, 27% of an 874 pt screen'. Severity major → minor. Also flag for whoever fixes it: on the house-first root reservesRootHearth returns false (:85) and the local Spacer is the ONLY clearance above the 83 pt bar, so deleting it unguarded under-clears that root.
confirmed.judgeNote: Facts verified (DailyRoomView.swift:371 Spacer 120 plus ContentView.swift:185 companionHearthReservation, which does apply to the flag-off root). Severity down from major: the surplus sits at the very END of the scroll, below all content, and the Companion dock occupies most of the reserved band, so the tester's actual experience is 'a bit of overscroll', not '27% of the screen wasted'. It is still a one-line deletion with no risk and it makes the bottom of the home feel deliberate. T1, bundled with B-47.

confirmed.title: Twenty hard-coded bottom clearances, none derived from CompanionHearthMetrics
confirmed.where: DailyRoomView.swift:371, ProfileView.swift:167, YourSpacesView.swift:97, CrossRoomView.swift:48, SettingsView.swift:164, RoomProjectView.swift:117, CollectionsView.swift:188,291, DesignerConsultationView.swift:46, DesignRequestStatusView.swift:126, MatchIntroductionView.swift:70, DocumentListView.swift:22, DailyStoryDetailView.swift:150, ThreadListView.swift:44, ProjectListView.swift:46, RecommendationsView.swift:278, ScanThresholdView.swift:142, ScanWalkView.swift:67,89,273
confirmed.evidence: Features/Money/MoneyScreenChrome.swift:14-20 names this exact defect and claims it fixed: "Each screen carried its own hard-coded bottom padding (120 here, 140 there) with no relationship to CompanionHearthMetrics.reservedHeight, so a change to the Hearth re-collides silently. One constant, derived from the metric." A grep for pinnedFooterClearance shows the metric has exactly ONE caller — MoneyScreenMetrics.bottomClearance — used only by money screens. The other twenty sites (values 100/110/120/180/190) were never converted. Real dock height is 140 and pinnedFooterClearance(houseFirst:false) = 148, so every 100/110/120 is 28-48 pt short: on the flag-off root the last row of Saved, Documents, Messages, Projects, Browse pieces, Design services and Your spaces sits under the Companion mark.
confirmed.fix: Replace all twenty with CompanionHearthMetrics.pinnedFooterClearance(houseFirst:) (or the reservation modifier where the screen scrolls) and delete the local constants.
confirmed.codeNote: Confirmed and it is the code root cause under A-88/R-07. `grep -rn pinnedFooterClearance` returns exactly three lines: the definition (CompanionSafeArea.swift:74) and two in Features/Money/MoneyScreenChrome.swift (:31 comment, :41 the sole caller). The hard-coded sites are there as listed — DailyRoomView.swift:371, ProfileView.swift:167, YourSpacesView.swift:97, CrossRoomView.swift:48, SettingsView.swift:164, DocumentListView.swift:22 and RoomProjectView.swift:117 (100) among them. The arithmetic checks out against the source's own constants: dockHeight = 64+4+44+28 = 140 (CompanionSafeArea.swift:39-40), pinnedFooterClearance(houseFirst:false) = 148, so every 100/110/120 is 28-48pt short. MoneyScreenChrome.swift:14-20 names this exact defect and claims it fixed — it was fixed for money screens only.
confirmed.judgeNote: Same defect as A-88 seen from the code side, and it carries the fix recipe (CompanionHearthMetrics.pinnedFooterClearance = 148 vs the 100/110/120 actually used at 20 sites). Keep as ONE work item with A-88; this row is the implementation checklist. The Money lane already proved the pattern, so this is adoption, not invention.

confirmed.title: The message composer is drawn under the Companion dock — threadDetail never yields
confirmed.evidence: ThreadDetailView is `VStack(spacing: 0) { ScrollView { … }; composer }` — the composer is pinned to the bottom edge with only .padding(.vertical, 10), no bottom safe-area and no Companion clearance. yieldsToPinnedFooter yields only for .invoiceDetail, .proposalDetail, .decisionDetail; .threadDetail (App/Coordinators/Coordinator.swift:100) is absent, so displayMode falls through to .resting/.nudging — the full 140 pt dock, centre-bottom, safeAreaPadding(.bottom, 28) (CompanionOverlay.swift:465-470). The composer is ~60 pt tall above the bottom safe area, so the charcoal mark lands on the "Type a message…" field and hit-tests it. CompanionSafeArea.swift:56-70 states the root safeAreaInset "does not reach a NavigationStack's pushed destinations", so nothing else protects this screen.
confirmed.fix: Add .threadDetail to yieldsToPinnedFooter (dock steps aside to the 44 pt corner mark) and give the composer .safeAreaPadding(.bottom).
confirmed.codeNote: The occlusion is real and shot-proven; the mechanism is half wrong. CONFIRMED: ThreadDetailView.swift:29-59 pins the composer with no Companion clearance; `yieldsToPinnedFooter` (CompanionSafeArea.swift:107-115) lists only .invoiceDetail/.proposalDetail/.decisionDetail, so .threadDetail (Coordinator.swift:100) falls through CompanionOverlay's displayMode ladder (:154-199) to the full 140 pt canonical dock at bottom-centre with safeAreaPadding(.bottom, 28) (:469-470); shots/C/26-dark-messages.png shows "5 THINGS NEED YOUR EYE" printed straight across the "Type a message…" placeholder and the mark breaking the composer's top rule. WRONG: it is not the mark that lands on the field — the mark's frame is y≈722-786 pt, the field's AX frame is {{30,799.7},{288,17}}; the overlapping element is the caption row. And it does NOT hit-test: CompanionContextProvider.swift:281-305 returns no nudge for .threadDetail, so displayMode is .resting, and in that mode CompanionHearthView.swift:167-170 draws the caption via the `else` branch — `.accessibilityHidden(true).allowsHitTesting(false)`. So this is pure visual occlusion of the composer, not stolen taps. "No bottom safe-area" is also imprecise (the default safe area applies; what is missing is dock clearance). Fix as written — add .threadDetail to yieldsToPinnedFooter — still correct.
confirmed.judgeNote: The worst finding in this area, and it is corroborated, not just code-read: C-13's own describe_screen of the thread screen lists the orb in the AX tree, so the dock IS drawn over threadDetail. Chain verified — ContentView.swift:197 puts CompanionOverlay() at root over the NavigationStack, and CompanionSafeArea.swift:110-116 lists only .invoiceDetail/.proposalDetail/.decisionDetail as yielding, so threadDetail gets the full 140 pt centre-bottom dock (dockHeight is documented in the same file as measured, not assumed). The composer is a ~60 pt pinned footer. A homeowner taps 'Message your designer', arrives, taps the middle of 'Type a message…' and the Companion opens instead — the app appears to refuse to let them type to their designer. The later sibling wins the hit test, so this is a hijack, not just an overlap. Not a blocker only because the trailing Send-button area and the field's left edge stay reachable. Fix is one enum case plus .safeAreaPadding(.bottom); it ships with the rest of the thread-screen pass.

confirmed.title: Scan and AR are gated to LiDAR-only iPhones; AR is gated more strictly than ARKit needs
confirmed.evidence: QuietConversationFlowHost.bootstrap() does `let hasLidar = RoomCaptureService.isSupported` -> RoomCaptureSession.isSupported, routing to `step = .fallback` (ScanFallbackEntryView, a typed-dimensions form) when false; RoomCaptureSession.isSupported is true only on LiDAR hardware. Separately ARPlacementViewModel.supportsAR is ARWorldTrackingConfiguration.supportsSceneReconstruction(.mesh) — also LiDAR-only, and stricter than needed: placing a USDZ on a detected plane works on any A12+ iPhone with plain world tracking, and ARPlacementManager.swift:40-44 already treats .mesh as optional (`if supportsSceneReconstruction(.mesh) { config.sceneReconstruction = .mesh }`). iPhone 17 (base), iPhone Air and iPhone 16e have no LiDAR — those testers never see the room scan and are told AR is unsupported for something their phone can do.
confirmed.fix: Relax supportsAR to ARWorldTrackingConfiguration.isSupported and keep .mesh as the optional upgrade the manager already treats it as; make the non-LiDAR path a first-class flow, not a "fallback".
confirmed.codeNote: Confirmed and rescoped. The unique, correct half is the AR over-gating, and I verified both sides of it: ARPlacementViewModel.swift:115-117 is `var supportsAR: Bool { ARWorldTrackingConfiguration.supportsSceneReconstruction(.mesh) }` (LiDAR-only), while ARPlacementManager.swift:40-44 already builds a plain ARWorldTrackingConfiguration with horizontal+vertical plane detection and treats mesh as an optional upgrade — `if ARWorldTrackingConfiguration.supportsSceneReconstruction(.mesh) { config.sceneReconstruction = .mesh }`. So the manager would run fine on any A12+ iPhone and the view model refuses first. The scan-gating half duplicates C7-10 (and A1-15); recommend scoping this finding to the supportsAR relaxation so the two rows do not both claim the NewRoomSheet fix.
confirmed.judgeNote: Same cluster as C7-10, but the AR half is a genuinely separate and unusually cheap win: ARPlacementViewModel.swift:115-117 gates supportsAR on supportsSceneReconstruction(.mesh) while ARPlacementManager.swift:40-44 already treats .mesh as an optional upgrade (`if supportsSceneReconstruction(.mesh) { config.sceneReconstruction = .mesh }`). Relaxing supportsAR to ARWorldTrackingConfiguration.isSupported is one line and hands AR placement to every iPhone 17 / Air / 16e tester who is currently told their phone can't do something it can. Do that one line in the same pass as C7-10's tile gate. The other half of the fix sketch — making the non-LiDAR path a first-class flow rather than a 'fallback' — is the real M/L work and belongs with B-30 in T2.

confirmed.title: No keyboard-dismiss affordance exists anywhere in the app (numeric pads have no exit)
confirmed.evidence: Six .numberPad/.decimalPad fields (a number pad has no Return key), including the 6-digit sign-in code at AuthenticationView.swift:327. Grep over all 589 Swift files finds ZERO ToolbarItemGroup(placement: .keyboard), ZERO .scrollDismissesKeyboard, ZERO endEditing/resignFirstResponder/tap-to-dismiss, exactly ONE @FocusState in the whole app (Collections/Views/SavedNoteSheet.swift:20,43,81) and exactly ONE .onSubmit (RoomSettingsView.swift:121). .submitLabel appears twice, both on search fields (ThreadListView.swift:110, ProjectListView.swift:107). So the auth form never focuses email on appear and never chains email -> password either.
confirmed.fix: One shared .keyboardDoneToolbar() applied to every numeric field, .scrollDismissesKeyboard(.interactively) on form scroll views, and a @FocusState chain on the auth form (autofocus email; Return moves to password / submits).
confirmed.codeNote: CONFIRMED — every grep count reproduced exactly. Zero ToolbarItemGroup(placement: .keyboard), zero .scrollDismissesKeyboard, zero endEditing/resignFirstResponder; exactly one @FocusState (SavedNoteSheet.swift:20), exactly one .onSubmit (RoomSettingsView.swift:121), two .submitLabel both on search fields (ProjectListView.swift:107, ThreadListView.swift:110); six numeric-pad fields at ScanFallbackEntryView.swift:173, ManualRoomEntryView.swift:65 and :133, RoomBudgetSheet.swift:61, RoomSettingsView.swift:193, and AuthenticationView.swift:327. One correction: the app has 435 Swift files, not 589. The auth instance is the load-bearing one — it is what puts P-22's Verify button behind an undismissable pad.
confirmed.judgeNote: Split the tier when planning: the 6-digit sign-in code field is T0 (a number pad has no Return key and it covers the Verify button that P-22 has already pushed to the sheet edge — that combination can end the only working sign-in path on production), while the other five numeric fields and the app-wide keyboard toolbar are T1. C1-37's auto-verify defuses the auth instance on its own, so if only one lands, land that.

confirmed.title: RoomBudgetSheet: a number pad inside a single fixed .medium detent with no ScrollView
confirmed.evidence: The sheet is a bare VStack (no ScrollView) with a .numberPad TextField at :60-61 and the Save button below at :76-85, presented with .presentationDetents([.medium]) — a single detent, so it cannot grow when the keyboard appears. SwiftUI keyboard avoidance shrinks the content region by ~291 pt of keypad, leaving ~146 pt of a 437 pt sheet on a 402x874 screen; the only compressible element is Spacer(minLength: 0) at :100. Combined with C9-08 there is no way to dismiss the pad either.
confirmed.fix: .presentationDetents([.medium, .large]), wrap the column in a ScrollView, add the Done toolbar.
confirmed.codeNote: Every structural fact verified. RoomBudgetSheet.swift:38-103 is a bare `VStack` with no ScrollView; the `.numberPad` TextField is at :60-61; Save at :77-87; `Spacer(minLength: 0)` at :102 is the only compressible element; there is no `FocusState`, no `.toolbar`, no `.scrollDismissesKeyboard` in the file (grep for presentationDetents/toolbar/FocusState in it returns nothing). Presentation confirmed as `.presentationDetents([.medium])` — a single detent — at RoomProjectView.swift:135. A numberPad has no Return key, so with C9-08 there is genuinely no in-sheet dismissal; the only escape is swiping the whole sheet away and losing the entry. Caveat for the plan: this is code-reasoned, not shot-verified — no screenshot of the sheet with the keypad up exists in the ledger, so WHICH element gets clipped (title/description at the top vs Save at the bottom) is unproven. That the layout cannot fit is not in doubt.
confirmed.judgeNote: Structure confirmed in source — bare VStack with no ScrollView, .numberPad TextField at :60-61, Save at :76-85, single .presentationDetents([.medium]). The arithmetic is not: Spacer(minLength: 0) at :100 absorbs part of the squeeze and nothing here is sim-verified, so 'Save is pushed off' should be measured before it is quoted. The load-bearing half is the combination the finding names in passing — a .numberPad has no return key, so with C9-08's missing Done toolbar there is no way to dismiss the keyboard, and that is a trap whether or not Save survives. Also gated behind creating a room first, so this is week-one, not first-five-minutes. Fix is S: add the Done toolbar, add .large, wrap in a ScrollView.

confirmed.title: LocalStoreClaimSheet is pinned to a single .height(320) detent its content overflows
confirmed.evidence: The only fixed-height detent in the app. Its content is all fixedSize(horizontal:false, vertical:true) so none of it compresses: 40 top pad + an h4 (22 pt Playfair) title wrapping to 3 lines on a 402 pt screen (~78) + 10 + a 4-line bodySmall paragraph (~72) + Spacer(minLength: 24) + 50 (Keep them) + 4 + 50 (Start fresh) + 28 bottom = ~356 pt against a 320 pt sheet. On a 375 pt SE-class screen the title and body each gain a line; above Large Dynamic Type it is far worse. This is the sheet that decides whether a guest's saved rooms and pieces survive sign-in.
confirmed.fix: .presentationDetents([.medium, .large]) (or .height(320) plus .large) and wrap the column in a ScrollView.
confirmed.codeNote: The setup is confirmed, the arithmetic is not. `.presentationDetents([.height(320)])` at LocalStoreClaimSheet.swift:59 is genuinely the only fixed-height detent in the app (every other of the 17 presentationDetents calls uses .medium/.large), there is no ScrollView, and every text is fixedSize vertical. But at 402pt (the audit's iPhone 17 Pro) the 50-char h4 title wraps to 2 lines, not 3, at 22pt Playfair over a 354pt column: 40 + ~56 + 10 + ~57 + 24 + 50 + 4 + 50 + 28 ≈ 319pt against 320 — it fits with essentially zero headroom rather than overflowing by 36pt. The finding is real one Dynamic Type step up, or on any 375pt-class screen, where 'Start fresh' is clipped out of reach on the sheet that decides whether a guest's rooms survive. Recommend re-severing as a Dynamic Type defect and confirming with `simctl ui <udid> content_size extra-extra-large` before the fix lands; the prescribed fix ([.medium,.large] + ScrollView) is right either way.
confirmed.judgeNote: My own arithmetic agrees it overflows: ~347 pt of non-compressible content (40 + a 3-line 22 pt Playfair title + 10 + 3-line body + 24 min spacer + 50 + 4 + 50 + 28) against a hard .height(320), the only fixed detent in the app. The clipped control is 'Start fresh', and dismissal is treated as 'Keep them', so nothing is destroyed — hence major, not blocker. Guest-then-sign-in is a common tester path and a visibly clipped decision sheet is the classic 'unfinished' tell. Worth a sim confirmation at default and XXL before the fix, since this is the one entry in the cluster that is reasoned rather than observed.

confirmed.title: aps-environment is `development` in the single shared entitlements file used for Release
confirmed.evidence: One entitlements file serves Debug and Release: <key>aps-environment</key><string>development</string>. A TestFlight build is signed for distribution and registers against the production APNs environment; a token minted under a sandbox entitlement will not receive production pushes, so every push-driven moment (proposal ready, invoice due, decision needed) silently never arrives and it looks like a backend fault. Only provable on a real TestFlight install — likely overlaps the A2-config lane, flagged here as a device-pass item.
confirmed.fix: Confirm what Xcode's distribution export actually writes; if it does not rewrite the value, split Debug/Release entitlements files.
confirmed.codeNote: The FILE FACT is real: Patina/Patina.entitlements:5-6 is <key>aps-environment</key><string>development</string> and one entitlements file serves both Debug and Release (CODE_SIGN_ENTITLEMENTS = Patina/Patina.entitlements in both configs). But the stated CONSEQUENCE is not supported, so severity major/testerVisible-true is wrong. Two reasons. (1) Xcode's App Store export re-signs with the distribution profile and rewrites aps-environment; nothing here proves otherwise, and no IPA has ever been exported. (2) The app already anticipates this: PushTokenService.detectEnvironment (Services/API/PushTokenService.swift:207-222) parses the embedded .mobileprovision per token and, crucially, returns 'production' when there is NO embedded profile — which is exactly the App Store/TestFlight case, since Apple strips it. Reclassify as a verification step folded into A2-07/A2-23: run `codesign -d --entitlements :-` on the exported .app and confirm aps-environment = production and no get-task-allow.
confirmed.judgeNote: Downgraded on new evidence the finder did not have. PushTokenService.swift:187-205 documents an explicit I66 ladder that parses the embedded .mobileprovision's aps-environment PER TOKEN at registration and never infers it from build configuration — the comment names this exact risk verbatim ('this project's Release signing has never performed a true distribution archive'). So the 'tokens recorded under the wrong environment' mechanism is already handled in code, and Xcode's distribution export rewrites the key besides. Add that push is on Kody's OWED list and not proven live for round one at all, and the tester-visible harm is speculative: major→minor, testerVisible→false. Resolve it for free inside A2-07's export inspection.

confirmed.title: INFOPLIST_KEY_UIStatusBarHidden = YES is inert; one screen hides the bar anyway
confirmed.evidence: SIM-VERIFIED from artifacts/ios-testflight-polish-2026-09-01/shots/steward/c-session.png (iPhone 17 Pro, 402x874): the status bar is fully drawn — "9:41", cellular bars, Wi-Fi, battery. The plist key is dead because UIViewControllerBasedStatusBarAppearance is not set to false anywhere (no such key in project.pbxproj or Patina/Info.plist), so the hosting controller's prefersStatusBarHidden (false) wins after launch. The app's own chrome agrees the clock is there: Design/Components/PatinaScreenChrome.swift:24-27 — "Reserves the status-bar region on a scroll container so scrolled content passes BEHIND the clock". Meanwhile exactly one screen, DailyStoryDetailView:51, applies .statusBar(hidden: true), so the clock pops in and out as a story opens and closes; on a Dynamic Island device hiding it does not remove the island.
confirmed.fix: Drop INFOPLIST_KEY_UIStatusBarHidden (the app clearly wants the status bar) and decide whether the story-detail hide is intentional — if so, apply it to every full-bleed hero, not one screen.
confirmed.codeNote: Substance confirmed — the status bar is drawn on every running-app shot and UIViewControllerBasedStatusBarAppearance is absent from both project.pbxproj and Patina/Info.plist, so the plist key loses to the hosting controller. One correction: 'inert' is too strong. The key DOES take effect on the pre-launch generated launch screen — shots/P/timing-1.png is a blank white frame with no status bar at t+1.26 s — which is why A2-14's flash reads the way it does. So the accurate statement is 'inert in the running app, live on the launch screen'. Overlaps R-08; keep whichever the synthesis prefers, but the DailyStoryDetailView.swift:51 pop-in/pop-out observation is unique to this one.
confirmed.judgeNote: AUTHORITATIVE on the status-bar question — the only sim-verified row in that cluster, and it corrects A2-11, C3-16 and half of R-08. I re-verified independently: shots/steward/c-session.png shows 9:41, cellular, Wi-Fi and battery all drawn. The remaining tester-visible defect is small but real: the clock pops in and out as a story opens and closes, and hiding it does not remove the Dynamic Island anyway. Drop the dead build setting, decide on the one screen.

confirmed.title: NewThisWeekRail: 160 pt fixed cards with no accessibility wrap — the only rail without one
confirmed.evidence: Both the image and the card carry .frame(width: 160, …), and the file contains ZERO references to dynamicTypeSize (grep -c = 0). The two other rails on the same surfaces both wrap to a full-width column at accessibility sizes: YourHouseRail.swift:172-181 (Layout.wrapped) and ProfileView.swift:253-259 (if dynamicTypeSize.isAccessibilitySize). Inside the 160 pt card sit Text(product.name).lineLimit(2) and a price line (NewThisWeekRail.swift:104-110), so at AX sizes a product name at ~32 pt in a 144 pt text column breaks to 3-4 characters a line and truncates — while the block directly above it has already reflowed correctly.
confirmed.fix: Give it the same Layout switch YourHouseRail has, or adopt containerRelativeFrame with the same 200-280 clamp.
confirmed.codeNote: All four cited facts verified: `.frame(width: 160, height: 112)` at NewThisWeekRail.swift:96 and `.frame(width: 160, alignment: .topLeading)` at :116; `grep -c dynamicTypeSize NewThisWeekRail.swift` = 0; and both comparison rails really do wrap — YourHouseRail.swift:174-180 (enum Layout) with `layout(for:)` switching on `dynamicTypeSize.isAccessibilitySize` at :190-192, and ProfileView.swift:253-259. Text(product.name).lineLimit(2) at :104-108 inside a 160 pt card with PatinaSpacing.sm horizontal padding is what truncates. One scoping caveat for the plan: A3-prod.md:277 records New this week as EMPTY on prod today (A3-01), so this only becomes tester-visible once the catalogue is populated, and then only at accessibility text sizes.
confirmed.judgeNote: Verified: grep -c dynamicTypeSize on NewThisWeekRail.swift returns 0, and the two neighbouring rails both wrap. The tester impact is the inconsistency more than the truncation — the block directly above reflows to a full-width column while this one keeps 160pt cards shredding product names into three characters a line, so on one screen the app looks both carefully built and carelessly built. Large text is common among the homeowner demographic; AX sizes less so. S effort, T1, ships with the other Dynamic Type work.

confirmed.title: Onboarding page 2's illustration is 280 pt tall inside a 190 pt band at accessibility sizes
confirmed.evidence: pageIllustration frames the ZStack to `dynamicTypeSize.isAccessibilitySize ? 190 : max(250, viewportHeight * 0.46)`, but phoneIllustration inside it is a hard .frame(width: 140, height: 280). .frame(height:) does not clip, so at accessibility sizes the shape overflows 45 pt above and below the painted gradient band and draws over the page title. Reached in production via ContentView.swift:73 -> OnboardingFlowHost.swift:81 -> OnboardingFlowView. It is the second screen a tester ever sees.
confirmed.fix: Scale the illustration to its band (.scaledToFit() inside the framed ZStack, or make the shapes relative to the passed viewportHeight).
confirmed.codeNote: Geometry confirmed, z-order wrong. pageIllustration frames the ZStack to 190 at accessibility sizes (OnboardingFlowView.swift:131-135) while phoneIllustration is a hard .frame(width:140,height:280) (:255-259); .frame(height:) does not clip and there is no clipShape, so 45pt spills above and below the sage band — and it is the second screen a tester sees, reached via ContentView→OnboardingFlowHost:81. Correction: the illustration is the FIRST child of the VStack at :103-114, so pageContent (title, body, dots, button) paints ON TOP of the spill, not the other way round — the title is not obscured; the shape bleeds out of its band behind the copy and above into the (hidden-status-bar) top edge. Not sim-verified at an accessibility content size; worth one `simctl ui content_size accessibility-large` screenshot before fixing.
confirmed.judgeNote: Minor because it only bites at accessibility Dynamic Type, but it is the second screen every tester sees and the shape draws over the page title — exactly the kind of thing an accessibility-using tester photographs and sends back. S fix (scaledToFit inside the framed ZStack). The art rework (C3-07) will touch this code anyway; make sure the replacement is band-relative rather than another hard 280 pt frame.

confirmed.title: ProfileView room cards keep a 140 pt hero even in the full-width accessibility layout
confirmed.evidence: roomList (:253-268) correctly switches to a LazyVStack of wide:true cards at accessibility sizes, and roomCard's own frame does grow (.frame(width: wide ? nil : 140) / .frame(maxWidth: wide ? .infinity : nil)) — but RoomCardHeroImage ignores `wide` entirely and stays .frame(width: 140, height: 100). Each card becomes a full-width block with a 140 pt photo stuck to the left edge and a large empty gutter beside it. Half the adaptation landed.
confirmed.fix: Thread `wide` into RoomCardHeroImage (.frame(maxWidth: wide ? .infinity : 140, …)).
confirmed.codeNote: Confirmed almost to the line. ProfileView.swift:346 `private struct RoomCardHeroImage` hard-codes `.frame(width: 140, height: 100)` at :362 (cited exactly) and takes no `wide` parameter, while roomCard does adapt (`.frame(width: wide ? nil : 140)` / `.frame(maxWidth: wide ? .infinity : nil)`) and roomList (:253-268) correctly swaps the horizontal ScrollView for a LazyVStack of wide:true cards on dynamicTypeSize.isAccessibilitySize. So at AX sizes each card is full-width with a 140pt photo pinned left and a large dead gutter — half the adaptation, as described. One nit: the call site is :287, not :286. Reachability confirmed: ProfileView is a real tester surface on both roots (ContentView.swift:344,351; TabRoot.swift:80; HouseFirstRoot.swift:274,281). Not sim-verified at an AX content size — code-truth only.
confirmed.judgeNote: Confirmed as a real half-landed adaptation, and the 'half the adaptation landed' framing is exactly right — roomList and roomCard both honour `wide`, RoomCardHeroImage alone ignores it. Two notes for the orchestrator. First, this is ProfileView, not a settings/account surface — it belongs in the browse-saved or visual-system area, so route it there rather than into the Settings pass. Second, it is only visible at accessibility Dynamic Type sizes; no first-round tester sees it unless they run large text. T2, and it is a genuinely satisfying one-line fix (thread `wide` into the hero frame) for whoever does the Dynamic Type sweep.

confirmed.title: Message bubbles capped at a hard 280 pt regardless of screen width or text size
confirmed.evidence: A literal 280, not a fraction of the container; the file has zero dynamicTypeSize references. On a 440 pt iPhone 17 Pro Max the thread reads as a narrow ribbon down the middle with ~160 pt of unused width; at accessibility text sizes a long message becomes a very tall 280 pt column of 3-4 word lines while 100 pt of screen sits empty beside it.
confirmed.fix: containerRelativeFrame(.horizontal) { w, _ in min(w * 0.78, 420) }, or drop the cap and rely on the 48 pt spacer.
confirmed.codeNote: Code fact confirmed: ThreadDetailView.swift:209 is a literal `.frame(maxWidth: 280, …)` with Spacer(minLength: 48) at :192/:210, and `grep -c dynamicTypeSize` on the file returns 0. But the magnitude and the picture are overstated, which is why I am dropping this to polish. On the 402 pt review device the usable bubble width is 402−32 padding−48 spacer = 322, so a 280 cap is ~87% of what is available and ~70% of the screen — right where iMessage sits. On a 440 pt Max the waste is ~80 pt, not ~160 (the finding subtracted 280 from the full 440, counting the intended 32 pt padding and 48 pt spacer as waste). Bubbles are also edge-aligned left/right (:191-212), so "a narrow ribbon down the middle" does not describe the render. The substantive half is the accessibility-size case — a fixed cap plus scaled type gives a tall 3-4-word column — and that alone earns polish, not minor.
confirmed.judgeNote: Half right. The width complaint at standard text sizes over-states: 280 pt on a 402 pt screen is ~70% of width, inside the normal chat-bubble proportion Messages itself uses, and the Spacer(minLength: 48) caps the usable width at 354 anyway — so the '160 pt of unused width' framing counts space that a bubble was never going to fill. No first-round tester notices this. The legitimate half is Dynamic Type: a hard literal with zero dynamicTypeSize awareness in the file turns a long message into a very tall 3-to-4-word column at accessibility sizes. Fold it into whatever accessibility-size sweep the fix program runs, and take the containerRelativeFrame form when it happens rather than scheduling it on its own.

confirmed.title: 78 pt fixed label columns truncate at large text (product spec rows, proposal sign sheet)
confirmed.evidence: Both are fixed-width leading label columns in key/value rows — .frame(width: 78, alignment: .leading) — and neither file has a dynamicTypeSize branch. "Dimensions", "Lead time", "Materials" at large Dynamic Type do not fit 78 pt and truncate or wrap into a ragged two-line stub against a value that did scale. ProposalSignSheet is a money screen.
confirmed.fix: Replace the fixed width with a Grid/ViewThatFits that stacks label over value once the label no longer fits.
confirmed.codeNote: Structurally confirmed: both sites are `.frame(width: 78, alignment: .leading)` (ProductDetailBlocks.swift:123, ProposalSignSheet.swift:98) with no dynamicTypeSize branch, and the label genuinely scales — PatinaTypography.mono/monoSmall are `Font.custom(…, size: 10/9, relativeTo: .caption2)` (PatinaTypography.swift:68,71) — with no lineLimit, so at accessibility sizes the label wraps inside 78 pt while the value grows beside it. Description correction: the product-detail labels are SIZE / LEAD TIME / MAKER / FINISH (ProductDetailBlocks.swift:113-117); 'Dimensions' and 'Materials' do not exist on that screen. Evidence-level flag for the plan: lane C ran XXXL and AX-XXXL passes over Today, Companion, Spaces, Studio and Settings (shots/C/ledger.md rows 30-38) but never the piece detail or the sign sheet, so this is compile-green inference, not sim-verified — cheap to confirm with one `simctl ui <udid> content_size accessibility-extra-extra-extra-large` screenshot of each.
confirmed.judgeNote: Confirmed as a real constraint in both files (78 pt fixed leading column, no dynamicTypeSize branch, and ProposalSignSheet's labels come straight from terms.lines so their length is server-controlled). Flag the coverage gap: this is code-inferred, not sim-verified — the walk captured AX-XXL for Today, Studio and Companion but never for the product detail or the sign sheet, so grab those before the fix lands. Impact is uneven and the plan should say so: a truncated 'Dimensions' on the spec rows is survivable; a truncated label next to the number a homeowner is agreeing to pay on the sign sheet is where trust actually lives. One shared Grid/ViewThatFits helper covers both sites, and this audience — homeowners and design clients, not developers — skews toward people who have raised their text size.

confirmed.title: PatinaTabBar's four-word row is arithmetically sized for a 402 pt screen
confirmed.evidence: The comment names the assumption: "Four words share one 402 pt row beside a fixed 54 pt slot". Row is .padding(.horizontal, 6) + four maxWidth:.infinity items + a fixed 54 pt trailing slot; each label adds .padding(.horizontal, 4), capped at .dynamicTypeSize(...DynamicTypeSize.accessibility2) with .minimumScaleFactor(0.7). On 402: (402-12-54)/4 = 84 pt per item, 76 pt of text box. StudioHubViewModel.apply() (Features/Profile/ViewModels/StudioHubViewModel.swift:81-97) coerces every failed source to empty — `projects: result.projects ?? []`, and the same `?? []` for decisions/proposals/invoices/documents/threads/notifications — then rebuilds `snapshot` from those empties, so a failed fetch IS a loaded-empty snapshot. The contradicting '5 things need your eye' comes from a DIFFERENT service with the OPPOSITE failure policy: BadgeCountService.shared.studioHint, whose apply() documents 'a nil argument means that fetch failed and its previous value stands — a stale floor beats a flickering zero'. (2) Severity blocker → major under this brief's own rubric (blocker = cannot proceed / crash / data loss / upload blocker; none apply — the tester can proceed and nothing is lost). (3) The fix sketch's 'give each Studio section three distinct states' overstates the work — a screen-level three-state design already exists (guest / loading / error at StudioHubView.swift:21-25); the defect is that the retry path can reach neither of the two non-content states. []`, so a source that FAILS is written back as zero — it does not preserve the last good value, contradicting the file's own header ('Partial failures preserve every source that did load'). confirmed.ledger: /Users/kody/Code/patina-merged/artifacts/ios-testflight-polish-2026-09-01/research/R.md (366 lines, full narrative + finding table). Shot ledger: /Users/kody/Code/patina-merged/artifacts/ios-testflight-polish-2026-09-01/shots/R/ledger.md (24 screenshots, all Read and judged).
confirmed.codeNote: BEHAVIOR CONFIRMED, ROOT CAUSE WRONG — and it is the keystone of this whole area. I reproduced the 400 against production Sanity using the exact URL the app's own URLComponents code emits (generated by compiling SanityHelpClient.buildArticleListURL's body in a Swift script, then curling it): HTTP 400, {"error":{"description":"expected ')' following function arguments","query":"... string::startsWith($sk, surfaceKey   \"/\"))] ...","type":"queryParseError"}}. The cause is NOT that $sk is sent as part of the query string — $sk IS sent correctly as its own query item (SanityHelpClient.swift:311-312), and Sanity accepts it. The cause is that the GROQ contains the string-concat operator `+` (SanityHelpClient.swift:307, `surfaceKey + "/"`), and URLComponents leaves `+` unescaped in a query value; Sanity's server decodes `+` as a space, so the query arrives as `surfaceKey   "/"` and fails to parse. Fix = percent-encode the query value (`%2B`) or restructure the GROQ to avoid `+`. Second correction: the fix's 'split the sheet's empty state from its error state' is already half-done — HelpPanelSheet.swift:151-158 renders a distinct PatinaErrorState with retry, it just never fires, because SanityHelpClient.fetchArticles swallows non-2xx and RETURNS [] rather than throwing (SanityHelpClient.swift:259-266); only InvalidSurfaceKeyError reaches the catch. Severity raised to blocker: this one encoding bug is why all six help doors are dead, so C5-02/C-04 cannot be fixed by authoring content. Confirmed independently of the Kong pause (Sanity is third-party; my repro ran just now).
confirmed.judgeNote: CONFIRMED and UNDER-STATED — this is the root cause of the entire empty-help cluster and I found the exact bug while judging. SanityHelpClient.buildArticleListURL puts the GROQ into URLComponents.queryItems; Foundation does not percent-encode `+`, and the query contains `surfaceKey + "/"`. Sanity form-decodes the raw `+` to a space. Reproduced against production just now: with a raw `+` → HTTP 400 {"type":"queryParseError","description":"expected ')' following function arguments"} showing `surfaceKey   "/"`; the byte-identical request with %2B → HTTP 200. Two consequences the ledger misses. (1) The article list can NEVER load, on any screen, on any build, for any surface key — this is not intermittent and not content-dependent. (2) fetchArticles (SanityHelpClient.swift:257-275) swallows non-2xx, transport and decode failures into `return []` AND caches the empty result, so HelpPanelSheet's loadError branch (:150-156, PatinaErrorState + retry, added for U29) is unreachable dead code — the designed error state cannot render. The finder's stated cause ("$sk sent as part of the query string") is wrong: buildArticleListURL:310-313 does pass $sk as a proper query item, and the sibling buildQueryURL:412 has no `+` and works fine, which is exactly why coachmarks and tooltips render while articles never do. confirmed.title: SwiftLint build phase is `|| true` — 421 error-severity violations never fail anything
confirmed.evidence:
shellScript = "if which swiftlint > /dev/null; then
  cd "${SRCROOT}"
  swiftlint lint Patina || true
else …". The phase also declares no outputPaths, so every build (archives included) prints `warning: Run script build phase 'SwiftLint' will be run during every build because it does not specify any outputs`. Standalone `swiftlint lint --config .swiftlint.yml` exits 2 with 421 error-severity violations, yet the Debug build was green — proving the phase enforces nothing. The .swiftlint.yml sets disallow_foregroundcolor / disallow_cornerradius / disallow_navigation_bar_hidden to `severity: error` on the promise that they gate.
confirmed.fix: Drop the `|| true` once the identifier_name bucket is resolved (G-11), and give the phase an output path so it stops re-running on every build including archives.
confirmed.codeNote:
Verified verbatim. pbxproj:408 shellScript = 'if which swiftlint > /dev/null; then
 cd "${SRCROOT}"
 swiftlint lint Patina || true
else …'; the phase (CBB2D0412F1D5E34007686CD, :392-409) declares empty inputFileListPaths/inputPaths/outputFileListPaths/outputPaths. The 'Run script build phase SwiftLint will be run during every build because it does not specify any outputs' warning appears twice in each of the Debug, Release and archive logs. G-lint.json has exactly 421 Error-severity violations (plus 512 warnings) and swiftlint exited 2. .swiftlint.yml does set disallow_foregroundcolor, disallow_navigation_bar_hidden and disallow_cornerradius to `severity: error`, so the 'promise that they gate' framing is accurate. ONE AGGRAVATOR TO ADD: because ENABLE_USER_SCRIPT_SANDBOXING = YES (pbxproj:585,649) and the phase declares no inputPaths, the in-build run cannot even open .swiftlint.yml — xcodebuild.log:12581 'The file ".swiftlint.yml" couldn't be opened because you don't have permission to view it. – Falling back to default configuration'. So those custom error rules are never loaded in-build, not merely swallowed by `|| true`; the fix needs an inputPaths entry for .swiftlint.yml as well as dropping `|| true`.
confirmed.judgeNote: Confirmed and WORSE than written, which raises the tier. `|| true` at pbxproj:408 is only half of it: .build/xcodebuild.log:12581 and research/G-unit.log:22813 both carry `The file ".swiftlint.yml" couldn't be opened because you don't have permission to view it. - Falling back to default configuration` (script sandboxing vs the `cd "${SRCROOT}"` read). The file is present and readable outside the build (apps/mobile/Patina/.swiftlint.yml, 2.7k). So the in-build lint neither fails nor even loads the project's own rules — the three error-severity design-system rules (disallow_foregroundcolor / disallow_cornerradius / disallow_navigation_bar_hidden) are not evaluated at all during any build. Severity down to minor (a tester sees nothing today; G-gate confirms zero current hits on those rules) but tier T1, not T2: the program that follows this audit is a UI-polish program touching dozens of view files, and running it with the design-system guard rails silently off is exactly how the visual system regresses between build 1 and build 3. Two independent fixes: (a) make the config readable to the phase (ENABLE_USER_SCRIPT_SANDBOXING / inputPaths entry) so the rules load, (b) drop `|| true` after G-11. confirmed.title: Permission strings are split-brained: build settings silently override the tracked Info.plist, and the shipped camera string omits QR sign-in
confirmed.where: apps/mobile/Patina/Patina/Info.plist vs the INFOPLIST_KEY_NS*UsageDescription build settings (dumped to research/G-buildsettings-release.txt)
confirmed.evidence: Both GENERATE_INFOPLIST_FILE=YES and INFOPLIST_FILE=Patina/Info.plist are set; the build settings win. Shipped NSCameraUsageDescription is "Patina uses your camera to walk through your space together and visualize furniture in your room." while the tracked plist's "Patina uses the camera to scan QR codes for secure sign-in and to capture your rooms" never reaches the binary. Same shadowing for NSMicrophoneUsageDescription (shipped "Have a voice conversation with Patina about your space and style." vs plist "Patina uses the microphone so you can speak with the Companion instead of typing") and NSSpeechRecognitionUsageDescription. The app really does use the camera for QR sign-in (Features/QRAuth/Views/QRScannerView.swift).
confirmed.fix: Pick one source of truth — the build settings already win — delete the shadowed keys from Patina/Info.plist, and rewrite the camera purpose string to cover both room capture and QR sign-in.
confirmed.codeNote: Fully reproduced against the as-built Info.plist. Shipped strings are the INFOPLIST_KEY_* wording: NSCameraUsageDescription = 'Patina uses your camera to walk through your space together and visualize furniture in your room.', NSMicrophoneUsageDescription = 'Have a voice conversation with Patina about your space and style.', NSSpeechRecognitionUsageDescription = 'Speak naturally with Patina instead of typing.' The tracked Patina/Info.plist wordings for those three ('...scan QR codes for secure sign-in...', '...speak with the Companion instead of typing', '...turn your spoken requests into Companion conversations') never reach the binary, while NSFaceIDUsageDescription and NSPhotoLibraryAddUsageDescription — unique to the file — do survive, which is why the split-brain is easy to miss. QR sign-in really does use the camera (Features/QRAuth/Views/QRScannerView.swift). Both GENERATE_INFOPLIST_FILE = YES and INFOPLIST_FILE = Patina/Info.plist are set on both configs, so the build settings winning is by design, not accident.
confirmed.judgeNote: major→minor on tester impact. The strings that actually ship are good — 'walk through your space together and visualize furniture in your room' is the right sentence for the prompt a homeowner hits first, and it is warmer than the plist wording it shadows. The finding's real worth is hygiene: two sources exist, one is silently dead, and the next person to edit permission copy will edit the dead one. Do that deletion at T1. Hold the QR omission as a Beta App Review 5.1.1 watch-item rather than a T0 risk — QR sign-in is a designer/Field path a round-one homeowner is unlikely to reach.

confirmed.title: Design-kit font bundle embedded twice (app + widget), duplicating ~1.4 MB of TTFs
confirmed.evidence: Both bundles carry the same ten TTFs — Inter Regular/Medium/SemiBold at 320 KB each, PlayfairDisplay Regular/Medium/Italic at 124 KB each, DMMono Light/Medium/Regular. Eight of the app's ten largest files are these duplicated faces. Invisible against the 69 MB Debug build only because Patina.debug.dylib is 64 MB of it; the Release app has no debug dylib.
confirmed.fix: Have the widget link the app's copy of the resource bundle, or ship the widget a trimmed face set — a widget needs one or two weights, not nine.
confirmed.codeNote: Reproduced from the built product: Patina.app/PatinaDesignKit_PatinaDesignKit.bundle/ and Patina.app/PlugIns/PatinaWidget.appex/PatinaDesignKit_PatinaDesignKit.bundle/ carry byte-identical face sets. Count correction: NINE TTFs per copy, not ten — Inter Regular/Medium/SemiBold (325/325/326 KB), PlayfairDisplay Regular/Medium/Italic (123/124/111 KB), DMMono Light/Medium/Regular (50 KB each) — about 1.48 MB duplicated, so the '~1.4 MB' figure is right. The 'a widget needs one or two weights, not nine' point stands.
confirmed.judgeNote: Correct at polish, with one reason to keep it visible: a widget extension runs in a tight memory budget, and a widget that exceeds it renders as a blank placeholder — which IS tester-visible on a Home Screen. Nine lazily-loaded faces will most likely never get there, so this is a watch-item, not a defect. The 'trim the widget to one or two weights' half is the better fix than resource-bundle sharing: a widget needs two faces, not nine.
